notes:
1. Investigated how to show "How It Works" beneath "StackShift II" in the Platform dropdown, and found the menu is a flat list in the content system, so nesting could not be done by styling alone.
  2. Built a full third menu level end to end — a new "link with sub-routes" content type, updated content queries in all thirteen places that fetch submenu routes, matching types, and the menu component — and prepared, but did not run, a content migration script with a dry-run mode.
  3. Addressed the concern that the migration would destroy production schemas: nothing had been written, schemas live in code and cannot be touched by the script, and it would patch one field on one document. Added an automatic backup before any write as extra safety.
  4. Scaled the change back at the user's request — fully reverted the schema, query, type, and script changes so only the menu component changed.
  5. Implemented a presentation-only grouping that indents any item labeled " - " beneath its sibling; when the menu then stopped showing, replaced it with a plain reorder that keeps the original markup and simply moves "How It Works" directly under "StackShift II".
  6. Verified in a headless browser against the running dev server that the drawer opens, Platform expands, items render in the new order, and there are no console errors.

notes:
1. Ran the production build to find why it was failing — a pre-build step stopped on one published article whose metadata contained an unescaped quoted word that terminated the text early. Confirmed the many long-standing type errors were unrelated because the build ignores them.
  2. Checked all published agent articles and confirmed only that one file was malformed.
  3. Escaped the stray quotes so the file parses, and reverted an incidental lockfile change that had crept into the working tree.
  4. Hardened the shared article reader so one malformed published file is logged and skipped instead of taking down the whole build, and verified the skip path with a deliberately broken test file.
  5. Re-ran the full production build — it now completes with all 783 pages generated, including every article page — and reverted build artifacts that only reflected the local environment.
  6. Answered how to prevent a repeat: the bug lives in the publishing tool that writes the files, not in the site, and the site has no gate between an automated publish commit and a production deploy.
  7. Gathered evidence for the publishing tool's defect — other articles have properly escaped quotes, so the tool usually works; the source post uses curly quotes, and the tool straightened them after the text had already been serialized, producing the invalid result. Recorded the diagnosis for the publishing team.

  2. Escaped the stray quotes in both affected lines and re-validated that the metadata now parses cleanly.
  3. Checked every other published article file for the same publisher defect and confirmed the damage was limited to this one file.
  4. Reviewed the file's change history to understand how the publishing tool had written the bad content, and confirmed an earlier build-error fix had touched the same file.
